question: Which trend describes how atomic radius generally changes across a period (left to right)?

solution.why_correct: Across a period, nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell, pulling electrons closer to the nucleus and causing atomic radius to decrease.
solution.why_others_wrong: A is the opposite trend (this happens down a group, not across a period). C and D don't reflect the well-established periodic trend caused by increasing effective nuclear charge.
solution.concept_recap: Across a period: atomic radius decreases (more nuclear charge, same shell). Down a group: atomic radius increases (new shells added, more shielding).

question: Assertion (A): Ionization enthalpy generally increases across a period. Reason (R): Atomic size decreases across a period, so electrons are held more tightly by the nucleus.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.why_correct: As atomic size decreases across a period, the outermost electrons are closer to the nucleus and experience stronger attraction, requiring more energy to remove -- directly explaining the increase in ionization enthalpy.
solution.why_others_wrong: B, C, D are wrong because both statements are true and the size-attraction relationship is the standard, direct explanation taught for this periodic trend.
solution.concept_recap: Ionization enthalpy trend: increases across a period (smaller atoms, stronger nuclear pull), decreases down a group (larger atoms, more shielding, easier to remove electrons).

question: Elements in the same group of the periodic table have similar chemical properties primarily because they have the same:

solution.why_correct: Elements in the same group share the same number of valence electrons (electrons in the outermost shell), which primarily determines chemical bonding behavior and reactivity, leading to similar chemical properties.
solution.why_others_wrong: Atomic mass and number of protons (atomic number) both increase down a group and differ between elements -- they don't stay constant. Number of neutrons also varies by element/isotope and isn't the basis for group similarity.
solution.concept_recap: Periodic table groups (vertical columns): same number of valence electrons, similar chemical properties. Periods (horizontal rows): same number of electron shells, properties change gradually across.

question: Electronegativity generally follows which trend across the periodic table?
options: Increases across a period, decreases down a group
Decreases across a period, increases down a group
Remains constant throughout the periodic table
Increases both across a period and down a group

solution.why_correct: Electronegativity increases across a period (due to increasing nuclear charge pulling electrons more strongly) and decreases down a group (due to increasing atomic size/shielding, making the nucleus less able to attract electrons from other atoms).
solution.why_others_wrong: B reverses both correct trends. C ignores well-documented periodic variation. D incorrectly claims electronegativity increases down a group, when it actually decreases due to increasing distance between nucleus and bonding electrons.
solution.concept_recap: Electronegativity trend: increases left-to-right across a period, decreases top-to-bottom down a group. Fluorine is the most electronegative element overall (top-right of periodic table, excluding noble gases).
